t: 3593 — Minimum Increments to Equalize Leaf Paths
o: Each root-to-leaf path's score must become equal, and we may only increase node costs. Increasing a node's cost raises every path passing through it uniformly. So the decision happens at branching nodes: among the subtrees hanging off a node, the deepest (maximum) path-sum defines the target, and each child subtree whose current max falls short can be fixed by raising that child's root node alone — one node per deficient child, which is clearly minimal since each deficient branch needs at least one increased node.
k: Increasing node v shifts all paths through v by the same amount, so fix deficits at the top of each subtree.
DFS returns the maximum root-to-leaf sum within a subtree; a parent targets the maximum among its children.
Each child whose value is below the sibling maximum contributes exactly 1 to the answer (raise that child node).

a.n: Approach 1: Post-order DFS with per-child deficit counting
a.i: Process the tree bottom-up. For node u, each child c reports the maximum path sum from c down to a leaf (assuming ancestors unchanged). Let M be the largest child value; every child with a smaller value gets its root node raised (cost 1 each). Node u then reports cost[u] + M upward. Summing one per deficient child over all nodes gives the minimum number of increases.
s: Build adjacency; BFS from root 0 to get parents and a processing order (avoids recursion-depth issues).
Traverse nodes in reverse BFS order; compute val[u] = cost[u] + max child val.
Feed val[u] to its parent: track the running max and count how many children fell below it, adding to the answer.
The answer is the total deficit count over all nodes (including the root's children).
a.t: O(n) — BFS ordering plus one reverse pass over all nodes
a.sp: O(n) for adjacency, parent array and per-node aggregates

w: Why raising the child root is optimal: any solution must raise at least one node inside each deficient subtree (its paths are short), and raising the subtree root fixes that entire subtree at once without disturbing siblings. Use 64-bit sums — path costs can reach 1e5 × 1e9. Iterative BFS-order processing avoids stack overflow on deep trees (path graphs with n = 1e5).
